title: Network Security
summary: How networks are attacked and defended: eavesdropping, spoofing, MITM and DDoS, firewalls and segmentation, TLS 1.3 in depth, VPNs and tunnels, Wi-Fi security, and detecting intruders with IDS, packet captures and flow logs.

lessons.title: Threats on the network
lessons.summary: Eavesdropping, spoofing, man-in-the-middle, replay and denial of service, including how amplification attacks multiply an attacker's bandwidth and how to calculate by how much.
lessons.body:
Basic IPv4, ARP, UDP and traditional DNS do not by themselves cryptographically authenticate every sender or encrypt application data. Checksums detect some accidental corruption, but do not prove identity. Security extensions and deployment controls can add protections.

Missing authentication and encryption enable several important network attacks. This lesson sorts those attacks into five families. For each one, ask two questions: **what security property does it break**, and **what is the standard defence**?

The classic properties are often summarised as **CIA**:

| Property | Meaning | Broken by |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Only the intended party reads it | Eavesdropping |
| Integrity | Nobody alters it undetected | MITM, injection |
| Authenticity | It came from who it claims | Spoofing, replay |
| Availability | The service stays up | DoS / DDoS |

(Strictly, CIA is confidentiality, integrity and availability; authenticity is usually grouped with integrity. It is listed separately here because so many network attacks target it.)

## Eavesdropping

**Eavesdropping** (passive sniffing) means reading traffic you were not meant to see. The attacker changes nothing, which makes it very hard to detect.

Where can an attacker listen?

- **Shared media.** Wi-Fi is radio: a nearby receiver may capture frames on a monitored channel, subject to signal, interference and radio capabilities. An Ethernet repeater hub repeated received signals onto its other ports, subject to physical-layer error and collision handling.
- **Switched LANs.** A switch normally forwards known unicasts toward the learned destination port, while broadcasts and some unknown traffic are flooded. MAC-table exhaustion or ARP poisoning may expose additional traffic, depending on switch protections and topology.
- **On the path.** Any ISP, transit provider, café router or compromised router between you and the server sees your packets.

Even when the payload is encrypted, **metadata** leaks: source and destination addresses, packet sizes, timing, and often the server's hostname (in DNS queries and the TLS SNI field, see lesson 3).

The defence is **encryption in transit**: TLS for application traffic, VPNs for whole networks, WPA2/WPA3 for Wi-Fi. The maths behind the ciphers is covered in the Security & Cryptography subject; here we care about where encryption sits and what it leaves exposed.

## Spoofing

**Spoofing** means forging an identifier. Many packet fields can be written by a sender. Whether a forgery is accepted depends on filtering, cryptographic validation and protocol state.

| What is forged | How | Classic use |
|---|---|---|
| Source IP | Write any value in the header | Reflection DDoS |
| MAC address | Change the NIC setting | Bypass MAC filters |
| ARP reply | Send unsolicited replies | LAN MITM |
| DNS answer | Race the real reply | Redirect a domain |
| Email sender | Set the From header | Phishing |

**IP spoofing** has a catch for the attacker: replies go to the forged address, not to them. So it is mostly useful for one-way attacks where the attacker does not need the answer. That is exactly what reflection attacks need (below).

An off-path attacker who cannot observe replies has an additional obstacle when forging a TCP handshake: the acknowledgment must match the server's initial sequence number plus one in the ordinary no-data handshake. Unpredictable sequence-number generation makes blind guessing harder.

> [!tip] BCP 38: stop spoofing at the source
> RFC 2827 (BCP 38) recommends filtering customer traffic against permitted source prefixes. This blocks spoofing outside those prefixes, but does not by itself stop one host impersonating another inside an allowed prefix. More granular source validation and reflector controls are also useful.

## Man-in-the-middle

A **man-in-the-middle (MITM)** attacker sits between two parties, relaying and possibly altering traffic while each side believes it is talking directly to the other. An unmitigated MITM can threaten confidentiality, integrity and authentication; correctly authenticated encryption can prevent reading or modifying protected content even when traffic is relayed.

```
 Normal:
 Alice ------------------------> Bank

 MITM:
 Alice ----> Mallory ----> Bank
   "I am the Bank"  "I am Alice"
```

Ways to get in the middle:

- **ARP spoofing** on a LAN: tell the victim "the gateway's IP is at my MAC".
- **Rogue Wi-Fi access points** ("evil twins", lesson 5).
- **DNS spoofing**: make the domain resolve to the attacker's IP.
- **BGP hijacking**: an unauthorised announcement may redirect traffic in networks that accept and select it.

Encryption alone does not stop MITM. If Alice does a key exchange with Mallory, she has a perfectly encrypted channel to the attacker. What stops MITM is **authentication**: Alice must verify she is talking to the real bank. In TLS that is the certificate check (lesson 3). This is why clicking through a certificate warning is so dangerous.

## Replay

In a **replay attack** the attacker captures a valid message and sends it again later. They do not need to read or change it.

> [!example] A replayed payment
> A client sends an encrypted, signed message: "pay merchant £50". The attacker cannot read it, but captures it and sends it ten more times. If the server only checks the signature, it pays out £550.

The signature is valid every time, because it is the same message. The defence is to make each message usable **once**:

- **Nonces**: bind a unique value to the authenticated request; atomically reject reuse in the relevant session or account.
- **Timestamps**: an authenticated timestamp can limit the acceptance window, but a replay inside that window still needs duplicate detection. Clock and expiry rules must be defined.
- **Sequence numbers**: authenticate counters and track accepted values. An ordered channel can require the next counter; an IPsec-style sliding window can accept unseen out-of-order packets while rejecting duplicates and packets that are too old. TLS early data has separate replay caveats (lesson 3).

## Denial of service

A **denial-of-service (DoS)** attack makes a service unavailable to legitimate users. A **distributed** DoS (DDoS) uses many sources, typically a **botnet** of compromised machines. The Mirai botnet of 2016, built from hacked cameras and routers, disrupted DNS resolution at Dyn and access to many customer websites.

DDoS attacks are classified by the resource they exhaust:

| Class | Exhausts | Measured in | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volumetric | Link bandwidth | bits/s | UDP reflection |
| Protocol | State tables | packets/s | SYN flood |
| Application | Server CPU / app | requests/s | HTTP flood |

### Volumetric

Fill the victim's pipe with more traffic than it can carry. If the link is 10 Gbps and 50 Gbps arrives, legitimate packets are dropped upstream, before your servers ever see them. You cannot filter your way out on your own equipment; mitigation must happen upstream, at your ISP or a scrubbing service (Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield) with sufficient capacity and filtering for the particular attack. Cloudflare reported a 29.7 Tbps attack in its [2025 Q3 report](https://blog.cloudflare.com/ddos-threat-report-2025-q3/); this is a provider-reported measurement, not a guaranteed limit on future attacks.

### Protocol

Exhaust a stateful resource with relatively little bandwidth. The classic is the **SYN flood**: send many TCP SYNs (often with spoofed sources) and never complete the handshake. Each one occupies a slot in the server's half-open connection queue until it times out.

The standard defence is **SYN cookies**. For a SYN handled with a cookie, the server avoids retaining a per-request half-open connection entry. It encodes limited information in the SYN-ACK's initial sequence number; the client's acknowledgment is that number plus one. The server validates the cookie and reconstructs connection state. Shared keys, counters and transient packet processing still exist. Firewalls and load balancers with connection tables are also protocol-attack targets.

### Application layer

Send requests that look legitimate but are expensive: searches, logins, uncached pages. A few thousand requests per second hitting a slow database query can do more damage than gigabits of junk.

**Slowloris** is the low-and-slow variant: open many HTTP connections and send headers one byte at a time, never finishing. Thread-per-connection servers (classic Apache) run out of workers. Defences include rate limiting, CAPTCHAs or challenges, caching, and event-driven servers or reverse proxies with short header timeouts.

## Amplification attacks

One important family of volumetric attacks combines spoofing with **reflection** and **amplification**:

```
 Attacker            Reflectors       Victim
   |  small query,       |               |
   |  src = victim IP    |               |
   |-------------------->|               |
   |                     | big response  |
   |                     |-------------->|
   |                     |  (x N)        |
```

1. The attacker sends a small UDP request to a public server (DNS resolver, NTP server, memcached instance), with the **source IP forged as the victim's**.
2. The server replies, to the victim, with a much larger response.
3. Thousands of reflectors do the same, all aiming at the victim.

UDP is used because there is no handshake to verify the source. The reflectors are innocent and the victim sees traffic from thousands of legitimate servers, which is hard to block.

### The amplification factor

The **bandwidth amplification factor (BAF)** is:

```
       bytes of response
BAF = -------------------
       bytes of request
```

The following historical examples use UDP-payload ratios. Rossow's 2014 measurements report sample means for particular queries and servers; GitHub's 2018 incident report cites an upper memcached example. They are not fixed protocol constants or current guarantees:

| Protocol | Approx. BAF |
|---|---|
| DNS | 28.7 (open resolvers), 54.6 (authoritative servers) |
| SSDP | 30.8 |
| NTP (monlist) | 556.9 |
| CharGEN | 358.8 |
| Memcached | Up to 51,000 in the cited 2018 report |

The attack bandwidth is then:

```
victim traffic = attacker upload x BAF
```

> [!example] Working it out
> A botnet has 2,000 devices, each able to send 5 Mbps. Under a payload-rate model with sufficient reflector capacity and no loss, total sending capacity is 2,000 × 5 = 10,000 Mbps = 10 Gbps. Reflected through open DNS resolvers with a BAF of 50, the victim receives about 10 × 50 = **500 Gbps**. Through exposed memcached servers even a 1 Gbps attacker could, in principle, generate tens of Tbps; in practice the reflectors' own links cap it. In 2018 GitHub absorbed a 1.35 Tbps memcached attack.

```python
def attack_gbps(bots, mbps_each, baf):
    sent = bots * mbps_each / 1000  # Gbps
    return sent * baf

print(attack_gbps(2000, 5, 50))
```

This prints `500.0`.

Two subtleties:

- **Headers dilute the factor in this unfragmented example.** A UDP datagram carried in one IPv4 packet with no options has 28 bytes of IP and UDP headers; link-layer overhead is additional. For a 40-byte request and 1,400-byte response, the payload BAF is 35, but counting only IP and UDP headers the ratio is (1,400 + 28) / (40 + 28) = 21. A full link-level ratio also needs framing and packetisation.
- **Packet amplification** matters too. One request producing many response packets multiplies the packets per second, which stresses routers and firewalls as well as links.

### Defending against amplification

- **Do not be a reflector**: close open resolvers, disable NTP `monlist`, never expose memcached (UDP 11211) to the internet. Memcached disabled UDP by default from version 1.5.6 after the 2018 attacks.
- **BCP 38** ingress filtering at ISPs, so spoofed packets never leave the attacker's network.
- **Protocol design**: cap amplification before validating a peer's address. QUIC permits up to three times the received UDP payload bytes before address validation; this bounds amplification rather than eliminating it.
- **Upstream scrubbing and anycast** to spread and absorb the flood.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> Universal attack-success rates, firewall mistake rankings and provider capacity guarantees are absent: this review has no representative measurement supporting those claims. Historical amplification figures above retain their original measurement scope.

## Key takeaways
- Basic packet identifiers are not cryptographic identities; validation and deployment controls determine which forgeries are accepted.
- Encryption protects confidentiality, but only authentication stops a man-in-the-middle.
- Replay protection needs authenticated freshness data and correct receiver state. A timestamp alone only limits the replay window.
- DDoS attacks target bandwidth (volumetric), state (protocol) or expensive work (application), and each needs a different defence.
- Amplification multiplies attacker bandwidth by the BAF; spoofed UDP plus a large response is the recipe, and source validation plus reflector controls reduce the available attack paths.

questions.prompt: An attacker passively captures nearby Wi-Fi traffic to try to read another user's data. Which security property is targeted?

options.text: Availability
options.explanation: Nothing is being disrupted: the attacker sends no traffic, so the network keeps working normally.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.explanation: Correct. Passive eavesdropping targets confidentiality. Capturing ciphertext alone does not necessarily reveal application plaintext.

options.text: Integrity
options.explanation: Integrity is broken when data is altered. A passive sniffer changes nothing.

options.text: Authenticity
options.explanation: Authenticity is broken by forging who sent something (spoofing, replay). Listening alone forges nothing.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask what the attacker *does*: receive frames only.
2. Nothing is changed, so integrity is intact.
3. Nothing is forged, so authenticity is intact.
4. Nothing is slowed down, so availability is intact.
5. The target is secrecy: reading data meant for someone else would violate **confidentiality**. Correctly encrypted ciphertext need not reveal its plaintext.

The defence is encryption in transit (WPA2/WPA3, TLS, a VPN). Even then, metadata such as addresses, sizes and timing still leak.

questions.prompt: For an off-path attacker unable to observe replies to the forged address, why is IP source-address spoofing well suited to reflection DDoS but poor for logging in to a remote server?

options.text: Routers detect and drop most spoofed packets, so only floods get through
options.explanation: Many networks still do not filter spoofed sources (BCP 38 is not universal), so spoofed packets often reach their target. This is not the reason.

options.text: Spoofed packets are always UDP
options.explanation: You can write any source address in any IP packet, TCP included. The protocol is not the limit.

options.text: Replies go to the forged address, so the attacker never sees them; a flood does not need replies, but a login does
options.explanation: Correct. Reflection wants the replies to land on the victim. A login is a two-way conversation, and the attacker cannot see the server's answers.

options.text: Spoofing only works on a local network
options.explanation: IP spoofing works across the internet wherever ingress filtering is missing; it is ARP spoofing that is limited to the LAN.

questions.workedExample:
1. The attacker writes the victim's IP as the source.
2. The server replies to that address, so the reply goes to the victim.
3. For reflection this is the goal: the victim receives the responses.
4. For a login the attacker needs the server's replies (including TCP's SYN-ACK and its 32-bit initial sequence number). They never see them, so they would have to guess, and modern stacks randomise the number.

So spoofing suits one-way attacks.

questions.prompt: Alice connects to her bank over a link that Mallory controls. Mallory performs a key exchange with Alice and a separate one with the bank, then relays traffic. Both channels use strong encryption. What would have stopped this?

options.text: A longer encryption key
options.explanation: Key length is irrelevant: Alice's channel is perfectly encrypted, just to the wrong party.

options.text: Alice checking that she is really talking to the bank, for example by validating its certificate
options.explanation: Correct. A man-in-the-middle is defeated by authentication. Assuming the trust store and bank credentials are uncompromised, Mallory cannot supply the required name-bound authentication proof, so verification fails.

options.text: Using TCP instead of UDP
options.explanation: The transport protocol does not prove identity. Mallory can relay TCP just as easily.

options.text: Compressing the data before encrypting it
options.explanation: Compression does nothing for identity, and compression before encryption has caused real attacks (CRIME).

questions.workedExample:
1. Encryption gives confidentiality *with whoever you did the key exchange with*.
2. Alice did her key exchange with Mallory, so Mallory can decrypt everything.
3. The missing step is **authentication**: proof that the other end is the bank.
4. In certificate-authenticated TLS, validate the certificate chain and bank name, and verify the server's proof of the corresponding private key. A copied public certificate alone is insufficient.
5. This is why clicking through a certificate warning hands a MITM exactly what they need.

questions.prompt: A botnet of 1,000 devices can each upload 2 Mbps. It sends spoofed queries to open DNS resolvers with a bandwidth amplification factor of 50. Assume those upload rates and the BAF both count UDP payload bytes, with adequate reflector capacity and no loss. What payload rate reaches the victim?

options.text: 2 Gbps
options.explanation: That is the attackers' own sending capacity, before amplification.

options.text: 50 Gbps
options.explanation: This multiplies 1,000 devices by 50 but forgets each device sends 2 Mbps.

options.text: 100 Gbps
options.explanation: Correct. 1,000 × 2 Mbps = 2 Gbps sent; 2 Gbps × 50 = 100 Gbps delivered.

options.text: 100 Tbps
options.explanation: This is a units slip: 2,000 Mbps × 50 = 100,000 Mbps, which is 100 Gbps, not Tbps.

questions.workedExample:
```
sent = 1,000 x 2 Mbps
     = 2,000 Mbps = 2 Gbps
victim = 2 Gbps x 50
       = 100 Gbps
```

Every byte the botnet sends becomes about 50 bytes at the victim. This is the ideal payload-rate result under the stated assumptions. A physical-link rate needs packet sizes, framing, packetisation and loss/capacity limits; its correction is not necessarily small.

questions.prompt: A reflector answers a 36-byte UDP request payload with a 1,200-byte payload. Counting 28 bytes of IPv4 and UDP headers per packet, what are the payload BAF and the IP-packet-byte BAF, excluding link-layer framing?

options.text: Payload 33.3, IP-packet about 19.2
Payload 33.3, IP-packet 33.3
options.explanation: Headers are added to both packets but are a much bigger share of the small request, so they lower the factor.

options.text: Payload 19.2, IP-packet 33.3
options.explanation: These are swapped: adding headers can only shrink the ratio here, not grow it.

options.text: Payload 33.3, IP-packet about 146
options.explanation: This subtracts the headers instead of adding them: (1,200 − 28) / (36 − 28) ≈ 146. Headers are extra bytes on every packet, so they are added.

questions.workedExample:
1. Payload BAF:

```
1,200 / 36 = 33.3
```

2. IP-packet sizes add 20 (IPv4) + 8 (UDP):

```
request  = 36 + 28    = 64
response = 1,200 + 28 = 1,228
IP BAF = 1,228 / 64 ≈ 19.2
```

3. The 28 bytes nearly double the small request but barely change the large response, so the real multiplier drops a lot. Rossow's cited measurements use UDP payload bytes. These computed sizes exclude link-layer overhead and assume one unfragmented packet in each direction.

questions.prompt: A client sends a signed message, "transfer £50 to account 1234". An attacker cannot read or alter it but captures it. Assume added freshness fields are authenticated and receiver checks update state atomically. Which measures prevent an identical request from being accepted twice, even within a valid timestamp window? Select all that apply.

options.text: Include a unique nonce the server records and refuses to accept twice
options.explanation: Correct. The second copy carries a nonce the server has already seen, so it is rejected.

options.text: Use a stronger signature algorithm
options.explanation: Incorrect. The replayed message is the genuine message, so any signature verifies. Signature strength is not the problem.

options.text: Include a timestamp and reject messages older than a few seconds
options.explanation: Incorrect as a complete replay defence: the attacker can resend within the accepted time window. A timestamp limits age but still needs authenticated duplicate detection.

options.text: Encrypt the message as well as signing it
options.explanation: Incorrect. The attacker never needed to read it; they resend the encrypted bytes unchanged.

options.text: Include a per-session sequence number that must increase
options.explanation: Correct if the counter is authenticated, scoped to the session and acceptance state is updated atomically. Strictly increasing acceptance rejects the repeated counter; sliding-window protocols instead track duplicates while tolerating some reordering.

questions.workedExample:
A duplicate must be distinguishable through authenticated freshness data and receiver state.

| Measure | Identical replay rejected? |
|---|---|
| Recorded authenticated nonce | Yes, including inside the time window |
| Stronger signature alone | No; original signature remains valid |
| Timestamp alone | Only after expiry, not within the window |
| Encryption alone | No; the same protected bytes can be replayed |
| Authenticated increasing session counter | Yes, with atomic acceptance state |

Neither stronger encryption nor a valid signature by itself guarantees freshness.

questions.prompt: For an incoming SYN that the server handles using a SYN cookie, what changes compared with retaining a conventional half-open queue entry?

options.text: It drops every SYN from an address it has not seen before
options.explanation: That would block every new legitimate client. Cookies allow eligible new attempts without retaining a half-open entry; filtering and resource limits may still drop SYNs.

options.text: It allocates a larger half-open queue
options.explanation: A bigger queue only delays exhaustion. SYN cookies remove the need for a queue entry altogether.

options.text: It requires the client to solve a proof-of-work puzzle
options.explanation: That is a different idea (client puzzles). TCP clients need no changes for SYN cookies.

options.text: It avoids a per-request half-open entry and puts a verifiable cookie in the SYN-ACK initial sequence number
options.explanation: Correct. The acknowledgment contains cookie + 1. After validation the server can reconstruct connection state; this saves half-open entries but does not eliminate packet-processing costs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Normal TCP: on SYN, store a half-open entry and send a SYN-ACK. Each entry waits for an ACK until timeout.
2. Spoofed SYNs never send that ACK, so entries pile up until the queue is full.
3. For a cookie-handled SYN the server does not retain a per-request half-open entry. It picks its ISN as a keyed hash of the 4-tuple plus a time counter and an encoded MSS.
4. When an ACK arrives with `ack = ISN + 1`, the server checks the hash and recreates the state.
5. Cost: some TCP options are lost or squeezed in, Linux tcp_syncookies=1 uses overflow fallback; value 2 requests unconditional cookie generation.

link.title: RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations

questions.prompt: Your data centre has a 10 Gbps internet link. A 40 Gbps UDP reflection attack begins. Why can't your own edge firewall solve this, however good its rules are?

options.text: Firewalls cannot filter UDP
options.explanation: Firewalls filter UDP routinely. The rules are not the problem.

options.text: The link is already saturated before traffic reaches the firewall, so legitimate packets are dropped upstream
options.explanation: Correct. 40 Gbps cannot fit down a 10 Gbps pipe. The ISP's router drops the excess, good and bad alike, before your firewall sees it. Mitigation must happen upstream.

options.text: Reflection traffic comes from legitimate servers, so firewalls must accept it
options.explanation: You could block the reflectors' source port, but it would not matter: the pipe is full before the firewall can drop anything.

options.text: Firewalls only inspect TCP handshakes
options.explanation: Stateful firewalls track UDP flows too; this misunderstands what they do.

questions.workedExample:
1. Volumetric attacks exhaust **bandwidth**, measured in bits per second.
2. Capacity in: 10 Gbps. Offered load: 40 Gbps (plus your normal traffic).
3. The bottleneck is the provider's router feeding your link. With a sustained 40 Gbps offered load and a 10 Gbps output, queues cannot absorb the excess indefinitely. Which packets are dropped depends on scheduling and upstream filtering; it is not necessarily three quarters of each traffic class.
4. Your firewall can drop attack packets, but only the ones that already made it through.
5. Fix: upstream filtering at the ISP, a scrubbing service, or anycast spreading the load across many sites with far more capacity.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce the internet's exposure to UDP amplification attacks in general, rather than just protecting one victim? Select all that apply.

options.text: ISPs applying BCP 38 ingress filtering
options.explanation: Correct. Filtering permitted source prefixes blocks external-prefix spoofing. Finer validation is needed to prevent impersonation within an allowed prefix.

options.text: Operators closing open DNS resolvers and disabling NTP `monlist`
options.explanation: Correct. Fewer reflectors means less capacity for attackers to borrow.

options.text: The victim adding a rate limit on its own firewall
options.explanation: Incorrect. This protects (at best) one victim from smaller attacks and does nothing about reflectors or spoofing; against a volumetric flood the link is full first.

options.text: Protocols such as QUIC limiting what a server sends before the client's address is validated
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC bounds pre-validation amplification at 3× received bytes. It reduces the amplification available to an attacker; it does not remove all reflection.

options.text: Memcached disabling its UDP listener by default
options.explanation: Correct. The 1.5.6 release disables UDP by default, reducing exposure unless operators enable it. Danger also depends on reachable capacity and configuration, not BAF alone.

questions.workedExample:
Reflection amplification needs a response directed to the victim and an amplifying service.

1. Source-prefix filtering limits who can be impersonated; within-prefix spoofing can remain.
2. Closing unintended reflectors removes those endpoints from the available pool.
3. QUIC bounds pre-validation amplification at 3×, rather than reducing it to zero.

These measures reduce systemic exposure. A victim-only firewall rate limit does not remove the reflectors or the upstream bandwidth bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A QUIC client's first Initial datagram has a UDP payload padded to 1,200 bytes, as the protocol requires. Before the server has validated the client's address, what is the most it may send in response to that one datagram?

options.text: 1,200 bytes
options.explanation: The limit is a multiple of what was received, not equal to it.

options.text: Unlimited, because QUIC is encrypted
options.explanation: Encryption does not prove the source address; anyone can send an Initial with a spoofed source.

options.text: 3,600 bytes
options.explanation: Correct. RFC 9000 caps the server at three times the bytes received until the address is validated: 3 × 1,200 = 3,600.

options.text: 14,600 bytes, one initial congestion window
options.explanation: The congestion window is a separate limit; the anti-amplification limit applies first and is far smaller here.

questions.workedExample:
1. QUIC runs over UDP, so a spoofed Initial is possible.
2. The server's handshake (certificate chain and all) can be several kilobytes, which would be an amplifier.
3. RFC 9000 §8: before address validation the server must not send more than **3×** the bytes received.
4. Clients must pad Initials to at least 1,200 bytes, which raises the cost of each probe:

```
limit = 3 x 1,200 = 3,600 bytes
```

5. If the handshake needs more, the server waits for more client packets or sends a Retry. Only receiving and validating the returned token establishes that the client could receive it; merely sending a Retry proves nothing.

questions.prompt: A thread-per-connection web server has 400 worker threads. An attacker on a home connection opens 400 connections and sends one header line on each every 10 seconds, never finishing the request. Real users get no response. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Buy a bigger internet link
options.explanation: The attack uses almost no bandwidth, so more bandwidth changes nothing.

options.text: Block UDP at the firewall
options.explanation: This is an HTTP attack over TCP; UDP filtering is irrelevant.

options.text: Enable SYN cookies
options.explanation: The handshakes complete normally. SYN cookies protect the half-open queue, not worker threads stuck on completed connections.

options.text: Put an event-driven reverse proxy in front with a short timeout for receiving complete headers
options.explanation: Correct. This is Slowloris. An event-driven proxy holds thousands of idle connections cheaply, and a header timeout drops the dribbling ones, so the workers only see complete requests.

questions.workedExample:
1. Classify: low bandwidth, completed TCP handshakes, incomplete HTTP requests. That is **Slowloris**, an application-layer attack.
2. The resource exhausted is worker threads: 400 connections each holding a thread.
3. Each connection stays just inside the server's idle timeout by sending a line every 10 s.
4. Fixes that target the resource:
   - Event-driven servers or proxies (nginx, HAProxy) that do not tie a thread to a connection.
   - A total deadline for receiving headers.
   - Per-IP connection limits.

questions.prompt: An attacker wants to forge a full TCP connection from a spoofed IP address and cannot see the server's replies. Roughly what is the chance that one guess of the server's initial sequence number, modeled as uniformly random across 32 bits for an ordinary no-data handshake is correct?

options.explanation: That is the size of a 16-bit field such as a port number. The sequence number is 32 bits.

options.text: About 1 in 4.3 billion
options.explanation: Correct under the stated uniform model: one exact guess succeeds with probability 1/2^32. The receive-window tolerance for established data does not relax this ordinary handshake acknowledgment requirement.

options.text: 1 in 2: it either matches or it does not
options.explanation: Two outcomes does not mean equal probability; there are 2^32 possible values.

options.text: Certain, because the ISN starts at 0
options.explanation: Predictable initial sequence numbers permit better-than-uniform guesses; unpredictable generation makes blind handshake spoofing harder.

questions.workedExample:
1. To complete the handshake blind, the attacker's ACK must acknowledge `server ISN + 1`.
2. They never see the SYN-ACK, so they must guess.
3. Under the stated ideal uniform model there are:

```
2^32 = 4,294,967,296
```

4. So a single guess succeeds about once in 4.3 billion.
5. Historically, predictable ISNs made this practical, which is why RFC 6528 recommends an unpredictable sequence-number generation method.

lessons.title: Firewalls, segmentation and zero trust
lessons.summary: Stateless and stateful packet filters, how rule order and connection tracking work, cloud security groups versus network ACLs, why flat networks get breached, and what zero trust actually changes.
lessons.body:
The previous lesson showed why receiving a packet does not, by itself, establish a trustworthy identity. A **firewall** is the first answer to that: a device or piece of software that sits on a boundary and decides, packet by packet or connection by connection, what is allowed through.

The second answer is to have more boundaries. **Segmentation** splits a network into zones so that a compromise in one zone does not hand over all of them. The third answer, **zero trust**, says that network location alone must not grant implicit trust.

This lesson works through all three, from the mechanics of a rule table up to architecture.

## What a firewall decides on

Every firewall matches traffic against a list of **rules**. The more of the packet it understands, the more precise the rules can be:

| Type | Looks at | Example rule |
|---|---|---|
| Stateless filter | Headers of one packet | Drop TCP to port 23 |
| Stateful | Headers plus connection state | Allow replies to my requests |
| Application (L7) | Protocol content | Block HTTP `POST /admin` |

Most rules are written in terms of the **5-tuple**: protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Add the direction (inbound or outbound) and the interface, and you can express most network policy.

### Rule order and default policy

The toy filter below uses **top-to-bottom, first-match evaluation**. Real products differ: AWS security groups combine allow rules, while nftables can continue across chains after an accept verdict. Anything that matches no rule gets the **default policy**, which should be *deny*.

```python
from ipaddress import ip_address, ip_network

RULES = [  # proto, port, source, action
    ("tcp", 22, "10.0.0.0/8", "allow"),
    ("tcp", 443, "0.0.0.0/0", "allow"),
    ("tcp", 22, "0.0.0.0/0", "deny"),
]

def check(proto, port, src):
    addr = ip_address(src)
    for p, dport, net, action in RULES:
        if p != proto or dport != port:
            continue
        if addr in ip_network(net):
            return action  # first match
    return "deny"  # default policy

print(check("tcp", 22, "10.1.2.3"))
print(check("tcp", 22, "203.0.113.9"))
print(check("udp", 53, "10.1.2.3"))
```

This prints `allow`, `deny`, `deny`. SSH from inside `10.0.0.0/8` matches rule 1. SSH from the internet skips rule 1 and hits rule 3. DNS matches nothing and falls through to the default.

Swap rules 1 and 3 and internal SSH breaks too, because the broad deny now matches first. Order bugs and broad rules that shadow narrow ones can contradict the intended policy. Good tooling flags **shadowed rules** that can never match.

> [!tip] Default deny, both ways
> Explicit inbound and outbound allowlists can reduce exposure. Egress restrictions can obstruct some command-and-control and exfiltration paths, but allowed services may still be abused; default-deny adoption is not universal.

## Stateless versus stateful

A **stateless** filter judges each packet alone. That causes a problem with replies. When your web server at port 443 answers a client, the reply goes *to* the client's **ephemeral port**, some random number such as 51,812. A stateless filter needs a rule covering the intended return traffic. For general public clients this often includes a range of destination ephemeral ports; source ports, addresses and protocol flags may further constrain a rule, but do not prove connection state.

A **stateful** firewall keeps a **connection table**. When it sees an allowed outbound SYN, it records the flow. Connection tracking supplies state that filtering rules can match. A known flow is accepted only when the applicable policy permits it:

```
 conntrack table (simplified)
 proto src:port        dst:port   state
 tcp   10.0.0.5:51812  1.2.3.4:443  ESTAB
 udp   10.0.0.5:40001  9.9.9.9:53   REPLIED
```

On Linux this is **conntrack**. This abbreviated nftables input-chain example explicitly accepts established and related traffic:

```
table inet filter {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority 0;
    policy drop;
    ct state established,related accept
    ct state invalid drop
    iif "lo" accept
    tcp dport 22 ip saddr 10.0.0.0/8 accept
    tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept
  }
}
```

This is an input-chain fragment, not a complete deployment ruleset: it omits IPv6 neighbour discovery, router advertisements, other required ICMP handling, and forwarding/egress policy. Blindly applying it can break connectivity. UDP and ICMP tracking uses protocol-specific tuples and timeouts; a UDP reply does not establish application-level authentication.

### The cost of state

State is memory, and memory can run out. The connection table is itself a DoS target: a SYN flood or many short UDP flows can fill it, after which the firewall drops new connections, including legitimate ones. Timeouts matter too. Linux keeps an idle established TCP entry for five days by default, while many cloud load balancers and NAT gateways drop idle flows after minutes, which is why long-lived idle connections mysteriously die unless they send keepalives.

## Firewalls in the cloud

AWS is a good case study because it gives you both kinds side by side:

| | Security group | Network ACL |
|---|---|---|
| Applies to | Network interface | Subnet |
| State | Stateful | Stateless |
| Rules | Allow only | Allow and deny |
| Evaluation | All rules together | Numbered order, first match |

Because NACLs are stateless, you must explicitly allow return traffic to ephemeral ports (AWS suggests 1024 to 65535). Forgetting the outbound ephemeral rule is a classic cause of "the security group is open but nothing works".

Security groups can also reference *other security groups*: "allow port 5432 from members of `sg-web`". Within supported AWS connectivity arrangements, the reference resolves to associated interfaces' private addresses and follows membership changes. It is a network policy reference, not cryptographic proof of application identity; traffic through a middlebox can require different rules.

## Beyond ports: application-layer firewalls

Port 443 tells you almost nothing in a world where everything is HTTPS. **Next-generation firewalls** (NGFWs) identify the application, user and sometimes the content. **Web application firewalls** (WAFs) sit in front of HTTP services and block patterns such as SQL injection.

Reading encrypted HTTP content requires authorised decryption, such as TLS termination or interception with a trust anchor accepted by the client. Some application identification instead uses exposed metadata; installing a root certificate alone does not intercept traffic. Interception breaks certificate pinning, adds a high-value target and can weaken TLS if the middlebox is poorly implemented. It is a trade-off, not a free upgrade.

## Segmentation

A **flat network**, where every machine can reach every other machine, means one compromised laptop can probe every server. An attacker may **move laterally** from the initial foothold toward other resources.

> [!example] The Target breach (2013)
> A March 2014 Senate staff analysis described an apparent path from compromised HVAC-vendor credentials into sensitive network areas. It cited Target's confirmation that around 40 million payment-card accounts were exposed. The report explicitly relied on then-available reports and expert analysis, not a completed public forensic reconstruction. Its segmentation lesson is to restrict supplier access to necessary resources rather than grant broad internal reachability.

Segmentation draws internal boundaries:

```
  Internet
     |
 [edge firewall]
     |
   DMZ: web, mail  ----x---- no direct path
     |                      to databases
 [internal firewall]
     |
 +---+--------+-----------+
 | App tier   | DB tier   | Corp LAN
 +------------+-----------+
```

- A **DMZ** holds internet-facing services, so a compromised web server is still outside the internal network.
- **VLANs and subnets** separate departments, guest Wi-Fi, IoT devices and management interfaces.
- **Microsegmentation** goes down to individual workloads: each service can talk only to the specific services it needs, typically enforced on the host or by the hypervisor rather than by a central box.

The design question is always **blast radius**: if this machine falls, what else can the attacker reach? Each allowed path is a possible route for lateral movement.

## Zero trust

Traditional design is **castle and moat**: hard perimeter, soft inside. In this simplified perimeter-only model, internal location grants broad trust; real perimeter designs can also enforce internal controls. That model fails when:

- An attacker gets one foothold inside (phishing, a vendor, a stolen VPN password).
- Staff work from home, cafés and phones, and data lives in SaaS and the cloud, so there is no single inside.

**Zero trust** (NIST SP 800-207) rejects trust based solely on network location. Its core ideas:

1. **Evaluate access to each resource** using subject and device identity and policy. NIST describes per-session access and ongoing reevaluation, not a requirement to make the user perform fresh MFA for every HTTP request.
2. **Check the device**: is it managed, patched and encrypted?
3. **Least privilege**: limit the resources and operations accessible for the task.
4. **Monitor and reevaluate**: collect relevant security telemetry and restrict or revoke access as risk changes. Shorter sessions limit some stolen-token exposure but do not automatically expire a stolen password or private key.

Google's **BeyondCorp** is an influential published implementation example, described in its 2014 paper. Employees reach internal applications through an **identity-aware proxy** on the public internet; being in a Google office grants nothing extra. Between services, **mutual TLS** can authenticate service identities, with authorisation enforced separately; a service mesh is one implementation option (lesson 3).

> [!warning] Zero trust is not "no firewalls"
> Zero trust adds identity checks; it does not remove network controls. Segmentation still limits blast radius when an identity is stolen, and an exposed management port is still exposed. Buying a product labelled "zero trust" while leaving a flat network behind it changes little.

## Pitfalls

- **Rule sprawl**: thousands of rules nobody dares delete. Tag each rule with an owner and a ticket, and review hits; a rule with zero hits for a year is a candidate for removal.
- **Any-any rules** added "temporarily" during an incident.
- **Forgotten paths**: management interfaces, backup networks and monitoring agents often bypass the segmentation everything else respects.
- **Trusting the VPN** as if it were the office (lesson 4).
- **IPv6**: a reachable IPv6 path can bypass IPv4-only filtering when a service listens on IPv6 and no other control blocks it.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> No ranking of the most common firewall errors, universal default-policy adoption rate or single zero-trust deployment recipe is supplied: the review has no representative measurement establishing those generalisations.

## Key takeaways
- Firewall evaluation semantics vary. The toy model is first-match; choose explicit defaults and needed inbound/outbound allowances.
- Stateful firewalls track flows so policy can allow matching replies; the state table is a resource attackers can exhaust.
- AWS security groups are stateful and allow-only; NACLs are stateless and ordered, so they need explicit rules for ephemeral return ports.
- Segmentation limits lateral movement; design each zone around its blast radius.
- Zero trust rejects trust based solely on location, evaluates resource access with identity and device context, and complements network controls.

## Further reading
- [NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final)
- [BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security — Google Research](https://research.google/pubs/beyondcorp-a-new-approach-to-enterprise-security/)
- [Control traffic to resources using security groups — AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html)
- [Control subnet traffic with network ACLs — AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html)
- [Simple ruleset for a workstation — nftables wiki](https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Simple_ruleset_for_a_workstation)
- [Firewall (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firewall_(computing))

questions.prompt:
A first-match firewall has these rules, then a default policy of deny:

```
1 allow tcp 443 from any
2 deny  tcp any from 198.51.100.0/24
3 allow tcp 22  from any
```

What happens to SSH (TCP 22) from 198.51.100.7, and to HTTPS from the same address?

options.text: SSH denied, HTTPS allowed
options.explanation: Correct. HTTPS matches rule 1 first and is allowed before rule 2 is reached. SSH skips rule 1, matches rule 2 and is denied.

options.text: Both denied
options.explanation: This assumes the deny for that subnet applies to everything, but rule 1 matches HTTPS first and first match wins.

options.text: Both allowed
options.explanation: SSH does not match rule 1 (wrong port), so rule 2 is reached and denies it before rule 3.

options.text: SSH allowed, HTTPS denied
options.explanation: This reads the rules bottom-up. First-match evaluation goes top to bottom.

questions.workedExample:
Walk each packet down the list and stop at the first match.

**HTTPS from 198.51.100.7:**
1. Rule 1: tcp 443 from any. Match. **Allow.** Stop.

**SSH from 198.51.100.7:**
1. Rule 1: port 443? No.
2. Rule 2: tcp any from 198.51.100.0/24? Yes. **Deny.** Stop.
3. Rule 3 is never reached.

If the intent was to block that subnet entirely, rule 2 must move above rule 1.

questions.prompt: What does a stateful firewall track that a stateless packet filter does not?

options.text: The application data inside each packet
options.explanation: Inspecting content is what application-layer firewalls and WAFs do. Stateful tracking is about connections, not payloads.

options.text: The user who sent each packet
options.explanation: User identity is a feature of NGFWs and identity-aware proxies, not of basic stateful filtering.

options.text: Which flows are in progress, allowing rules to match connection state
options.explanation: Correct. State provides context for policy. An established/related accept rule can permit return traffic without a separate port-range rule, but tracking alone does not bypass filtering.

options.text: The physical port each packet arrived on
options.explanation: Even stateless filters can match on the interface; that is not what state means.

questions.workedExample:
1. Stateless: each packet is judged in isolation against the rules.
2. Stateful: on the first allowed packet (say an outbound SYN), the firewall records the flow: protocol, addresses, ports, state.
3. Later packets may match established or related state. Whether they are accepted depends on the applicable rules; not every recorded packet is established.
4. That is why the nftables ruleset starts with `ct state established,related accept`.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the zero trust model?

options.text: Remove firewalls and rely entirely on encryption
options.explanation: Zero trust keeps network controls; it adds identity checks rather than replacing segmentation.

options.text: Trust nothing from the internet, but trust everything on the internal network
options.explanation: That is the castle-and-moat model zero trust rejects.

options.text: Require a VPN for every connection
options.explanation: A VPN can coexist with zero trust, but a tunnel alone does not provide per-resource authentication and authorisation.

options.text: Do not grant implicit trust solely from network location; evaluate resource access using identity, device and policy
options.explanation: Correct. NIST SP 800-207 defines zero trust as removing implicit trust in network location and evaluating every access request.

questions.workedExample:
1. Old model: inside = trusted. One foothold inside unlocks everything.
2. Zero trust: being on the office LAN or VPN grants nothing by itself.
3. Each request is checked: who is the user, which service, is the device managed and patched, is this access needed?
4. Access is scoped to the resources and operations required for a session, with reevaluation as policy dictates.
5. Network segmentation still exists, to limit blast radius if an identity is stolen.

questions.prompt: An EC2 web server's security group allows inbound TCP 443 from anywhere. Its subnet's custom network ACL allows inbound TCP 443 and outbound TCP 443, and nothing else (the final rule denies everything). Clients cannot load the site. Why?

options.text: Security groups are stateless, so replies need their own rule
options.explanation: Security groups are stateful; replies to allowed inbound traffic are automatic at that layer.

options.text: The NACL is stateless, and replies go to clients' ephemeral ports, not to 443, so they are denied outbound
options.explanation: Correct. The server replies from 443 to ports such as 51,812. The NACL has no outbound rule for those ports. Add an outbound allow for TCP 1024–65535.

options.text: NACL rules are ignored when a security group exists
options.explanation: Both apply: traffic must pass the subnet's NACL and the interface's security group.

options.text: The NACL must also allow inbound ephemeral ports for the requests to arrive
options.explanation: The requests arrive on port 443, which is allowed. It is the outbound replies to ephemeral ports that fail.

questions.workedExample:
Trace one connection from client port 51812:

```
in : client:51812 -> srv:443
     NACL in 443   allow
     SG   in 443   allow
out: srv:443 -> client:51812
     SG   stateful, allow
     NACL out 51812? no rule
     -> DENY
```

The NACL judges the reply as a fresh packet with destination port 51,812. Fix: outbound NACL rule allowing TCP 1024–65535 to 0.0.0.0/0.

questions.prompt: Which statements about AWS security groups and network ACLs are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Security groups support only allow rules
options.explanation: Correct. Security groups have no explicit deny rules. For traffic they filter, unmatched new traffic is denied; documented exceptions such as Amazon-provided DNS are not blocked by security groups.

options.text: Network ACL rules are evaluated in number order, and the first match applies
options.explanation: Correct. That is why rule numbering (100, 200, ...) leaves gaps for inserting rules later.

options.text: Security group rules are evaluated in the order they were created
options.explanation: Incorrect. All security group rules are evaluated together; since they are all allows, order cannot matter.

options.text: A security group rule can allow traffic from members of another security group
options.explanation: Correct within supported AWS arrangements. A source-group reference permits traffic from associated interfaces' private addresses; middlebox routing and connectivity restrictions matter.

options.text: Network ACLs apply to individual network interfaces
options.explanation: Incorrect. NACLs apply at the subnet boundary; security groups apply to interfaces.

questions.workedExample:
| | SG | NACL |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Interface | Subnet |
| State | Stateful | Stateless |
| Deny rules | No | Yes |
| Order | All together | Lowest number first |

A practical pattern: use security groups for almost everything (with group references for app-to-DB paths), and NACLs for coarse subnet-wide denies such as blocking a known-bad range.

questions.prompt: An attacker phishes one employee's laptop on a flat corporate network. Which control most directly limits how far they can go from there?

options.text: A stronger edge firewall at the internet boundary
options.explanation: The attacker is already inside; the edge firewall is behind them.

options.text: Internal segmentation, so the laptop's network can reach only the services it needs
options.explanation: Correct. Segmentation shrinks the blast radius: the laptop cannot probe database servers or management interfaces it has no business reaching.

options.text: A DDoS scrubbing service
options.explanation: Scrubbing protects availability against floods; it does nothing about an intruder moving laterally.

options.text: Longer passwords for the Wi-Fi network
options.explanation: The laptop is already connected; Wi-Fi authentication strength does not limit what it can reach.

questions.workedExample:
1. On a flat network the laptop can reach every host: file servers, databases, domain controllers.
2. The attacker's next step is **lateral movement**: scan, find a weak service, pivot.
3. Segmentation puts a policy point between the user zone and the server zones, allowing only, say, HTTPS to the intranet.
4. Traffic outside the allowed paths hits a deny rule. Logs or alerts appear only if monitoring is configured; permitted services still need protection.
5. Zero trust goes further by requiring identity per request, but segmentation is the direct network control.

questions.prompt: During an attack, a stateful firewall in front of a busy service starts dropping new legitimate connections even though its CPU and links are fine. Its logs show the connection table at its maximum size. What attack is most likely, and what is a sensible mitigation?

options.text: A Slowloris attack; add more worker threads to the firewall
options.explanation: Slowloris targets application workers on the server. And firewalls do not have HTTP worker threads to add.

options.text: A volumetric attack; buy more bandwidth
options.explanation: The links are fine, so bandwidth is not the exhausted resource.

options.text: A state-exhaustion flood; use protocol-appropriate admission controls, such as correctly configured SYN proxying for TCP, and review tracking limits/timeouts
options.explanation: Correct. SYN proxying must avoid allocating normal tracked state for unverified SYNs. Host TCP cookies alone may leave a separate firewall table exposed; UDP floods need different controls.

options.text: DNS spoofing; enable DNSSEC
options.explanation: DNS spoofing redirects clients; it does not fill a firewall's table.

questions.workedExample:
1. A full connection table can reject new flows despite spare link capacity.
2. Identify which protocol and state entries are consuming it.
3. For SYN floods, a correctly configured SYN proxy can validate clients before normal tracked-state allocation; nftables examples combine notrack and synproxy.
4. Tune limits/timeouts within memory and service requirements; a larger table alone is not prevention.
5. Selective tracking bypass may suit some traffic only with an explicit stateless policy and no required stateful NAT/dependent rules. It is not a blanket DNS fix.

questions.prompt: A host's nftables input chain has `policy drop`, a rule `tcp dport 22 ip saddr 10.0.0.0/8 accept`, and an accept for TCP 80 and 443. The host also has a global IPv6 address. Using the `inet` family, what happens to SSH from an internet IPv6 address?

options.text: It is accepted, because the SSH rule only mentions IPv4
options.explanation: Rules that do not match fall through; they do not accept. The SSH rule fails to match IPv6, so the packet continues to the default.

options.text: It is dropped, because no rule matches and the chain policy is drop
options.explanation: Correct. `ip saddr` matches only IPv4 packets, so IPv6 SSH matches no accept rule and gets the drop policy. Note that with an `ip`-only table and no IPv6 filtering at all, this IPv4 ruleset would provide no IPv6 protection; actual reachability still depends on routes, listeners and other controls.

options.text: It is rejected with an ICMP error
options.explanation: `policy drop` silently drops; sending an error needs an explicit `reject` rule.

options.text: It is accepted as `ct state established`
options.explanation: A new SSH connection is not yet established; the first SYN is state `new`.

questions.workedExample:
1. `table inet` handles both IPv4 and IPv6 packets.
2. Packet: TCP SYN to port 22, IPv6 source.
3. `ct state established,related`: no, it is new.
4. `tcp dport 22 ip saddr 10.0.0.0/8`: `ip saddr` only matches IPv4, so no.
5. `tcp dport {80,443}`: no.
6. End of chain: `policy drop`.

The pitfall the lesson warns about is the other configuration: rules written only for IPv4 (old `iptables` without `ip6tables`) leave the IPv6 address completely unfiltered.

questions.prompt: You are moving an internal admin dashboard from "VPN only" to a zero trust design. Which changes are consistent with zero trust? Select all that apply.

options.text: Put the dashboard behind an identity-aware proxy that validates requests against the user's authenticated SSO session and applies MFA/reauthentication according to policy
options.explanation: Correct. Access is decided per request by identity, not by having a tunnel into the network.

options.text: Require the device to be company-managed and patched before access is granted
options.explanation: Correct. Device posture is a core zero trust signal alongside user identity.

options.text: Allow anyone whose source IP is in the office range without login
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is location-based trust, the exact thing zero trust removes.

options.text: Keep the dashboard's servers in a segment that only the proxy can reach
options.explanation: Correct. Zero trust complements segmentation; the proxy is the single enforced path, which limits blast radius.

options.text: Remove logging, since every request is now authenticated
options.explanation: Incorrect. "Assume breach" means logging and monitoring every access, because credentials can still be stolen.

questions.workedExample:
Check each option against the principles:

| Option | Principle | OK? |
|---|---|---|
| Identity proxy, MFA | Per-request auth | Yes |
| Managed device | Device posture | Yes |
| Office IP bypass | Location trust | No |
| Segment behind proxy | Least privilege | Yes |
| Remove logging | Assume breach | No |

The result looks like BeyondCorp: the proxy is reachable from anywhere, but what it lets through depends on who and what is asking.

questions.prompt:
Your firewall review tool flags rule 3 below as **shadowed**. Why?

```
1 allow tcp 80,443 from any
2 deny  tcp any    from 0.0.0.0/0
3 allow tcp 8443   from 10.0.0.0/8
```

options.text: Rule 3 is too narrow to ever be useful
options.explanation: Narrow rules are good. The issue is that it can never be reached.

options.text: Rule 3 is redundant because rule 1 already allows port 8443
options.explanation: Rule 1 covers only 80 and 443, not 8443.

options.text: Every packet rule 3 would match has already matched rule 2, so rule 3 can never take effect
options.explanation: Correct. TCP to 8443 from 10.0.0.0/8 is a subset of "TCP to any port from anywhere", which rule 2 denies first. The intended internal access is silently blocked.

options.text: Rule 3 conflicts with the default policy
options.explanation: The default policy only applies when no rule matches; here rule 2 matches first.

questions.workedExample:
1. A rule is **shadowed** when an earlier rule matches every packet it could match.
2. Rule 3 matches: TCP, port 8443, source in 10.0.0.0/8.
3. Rule 2 matches: TCP, any port, any source. That is a superset.
4. So any packet that could reach rule 3 is denied by rule 2 first.
5. Fix: move rule 3 above rule 2. With first-match semantics, put specific rules above broad ones.

questions.prompt: A long-lived database connection through a cloud NAT gateway sits idle for 10 minutes, then the next query hangs and eventually fails. The database never closed the connection. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

options.text: The database ran out of connections; raise `max_connections`
options.explanation: The database still considers the connection open; it was not refused.

options.text: The TCP initial sequence number expired; reconnect every 5 minutes
options.explanation: ISNs do not expire. This invents a mechanism.

options.text: TLS session keys expire after 10 minutes
options.explanation: TLS sessions do not silently die after idle periods like this; the symptom is a dropped flow, not a crypto error.

options.text: The NAT or firewall dropped the idle flow from its state table; enable TCP keepalives with an interval shorter than the idle timeout
options.explanation: Correct as a likely class of cause. Devices vary: AWS NAT Gateway times out after 350 idle seconds and returns RST when an internal client continues. Keepalive timing must refresh the relevant state before expiry.

questions.workedExample:
1. Middleboxes with connection tables must eventually forget idle flows, or the table fills.
2. Each has an idle timeout. AWS NAT Gateway: 350 s. Linux conntrack: 5 days by default. Different devices, very different numbers.
3. After 10 idle minutes the NAT's entry is gone.
4. The next query's packets match no entry and are dropped (or answered with a RST), so failure can be immediate on RST or delayed after silent dropping, depending on the device.
5. Fix: TCP keepalives (or application pings) every, say, 60 s, and connection pools that validate connections before use.

lessons.title: TLS 1.3, certificates, ECH and mTLS
lessons.summary: What happens in a TLS 1.3 handshake and why each message is there, how certificate chains are validated and revoked, what Encrypted Client Hello hides, and how mutual TLS authenticates both ends.
lessons.body:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol behind the padlock: HTTPS and configured secure SMTP/IMAP use TLS. QUIC version 1 uses the TLS 1.3 handshake for authentication and key establishment, while QUIC applies its own packet protection. Lesson 1 showed that encryption alone does not stop a man-in-the-middle; you also need to know *who* you are talking to. Correctly configured TLS can provide both; peer verification and the negotiated authentication mode matter.

This lesson takes the network engineer's view: what is on the wire, what each message proves, and what goes wrong in production. How the ciphers and key exchanges work mathematically is covered in the Security & Cryptography subject.

## What TLS does and does not protect

TLS gives a connection three properties:

- **Confidentiality**: only the two endpoints can read the data.
- **Integrity**: protected records reject unauthorised changes under the cryptographic assumptions; this does not prevent packet loss, delay or all denial of service.
- **Authentication**: in the certificate-based mode below, the client validates the server identity and proof of its private key. PSK modes use a different credential. Client certificate authentication is optional (mTLS, below).

It does **not** hide:

- IP addresses and ports (they are in the IP and TCP headers).
- Sizes and timing of records, which can leak which page you visited.
- Traditionally, the hostname, sent in clear in the **SNI** (Server Name Indication) extension so a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to present. ECH fixes this (below).

## Why TLS 1.3 was needed

The pre-TLS-1.3 ecosystem retained legacy protocol versions, cipher suites and implementations with weaknesses. TLS 1.2 CBC suites were exposed to timing and padding-oracle implementation attacks; original POODLE targeted SSL 3.0. RSA key transport also lacks forward secrecy: later compromise of its decryption key can expose recorded handshakes using that key. A conventional full TLS 1.2 handshake takes two TLS round trips before client application data, excluding TCP setup and False Start.

TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) took a hard line:

| Removed | Why |
|---|---|
| RSA key transport, static DH | No forward secrecy |
| CBC modes, RC4 | Padding and bias attacks |
| SHA-1, MD5 in signatures | Collisions |
| Compression | CRIME attack |
| Renegotiation | Complex, attacked |

What is left is small. RFC 8446 originally defines five cipher suites, all **AEAD** (authenticated encryption), the common ones being `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`, `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384` and `TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256`. Certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral key establishment. RFC 8446 also permits PSK-only `psk_ke`, which lacks forward secrecy against later PSK compromise; PSK with ephemeral DH can provide it for post-handshake traffic. Early data has separate limitations below. Secure erasure of ephemeral/session secrets is part of the model.

## The 1-RTT handshake

This diagram shows a full certificate-authenticated handshake without HelloRetryRequest, client certificates or early data. It excludes TCP setup; implementation scheduling and transport loss can add delay.

```
Client                       Server
ClientHello
 key_share, SNI, ALPN  ------>
                        ServerHello
                         key_share
             {EncryptedExtensions}
                     {Certificate}
               {CertificateVerify}
                        {Finished}
                     <------
{Finished}             ------>
[app data]   <------>  [app data]

{ } = encrypted with handshake keys
[ ] = encrypted with traffic keys
```

Step by step:

1. **ClientHello.** The client lists versions, cipher suites and signature algorithms, and, crucially, sends a **key share** straight away. It guesses which group the server will accept (for example, X25519 when supported). It also sends SNI and ALPN (for example `h2` for HTTP/2).
2. **ServerHello.** The server picks the options and sends its own key share. Both sides can now compute a shared secret, and subsequent handshake messages in this flow are encrypted; record headers and optional compatibility ChangeCipherSpec records are exceptions.
3. **EncryptedExtensions**: the rest of the server's choices, such as the agreed ALPN.
4. **Certificate**: the server's certificate chain. In TLS 1.2 this went in clear; now a passive observer cannot see which certificate was presented.
5. **CertificateVerify**: a signature using the certificate's private key over a context-bound transcript value (including a fixed prefix, role-specific context string and transcript hash). This proves the server holds the key *right now*, and binds the key exchange to that identity, which is what defeats a man-in-the-middle.
6. **Finished**: a MAC over the whole transcript. If an attacker altered any earlier message (say, deleted the strongest cipher suites to force a weak one), the transcripts differ and Finished fails.

The client sends its own Finished and can send application data immediately in this successful flow: one TLS round trip versus two for the conventional full TLS 1.2 flow.

If the client guessed the wrong group, the server replies with a **HelloRetryRequest** naming one it supports, costing an extra round trip.

### Downgrade protection and ossification

A downgrade can expose older protocol choices or weaker permitted configurations; a correctly configured TLS 1.2 connection is not automatically vulnerable to every historical attack. So a TLS 1.3 server that ends up negotiating 1.2 puts a fixed sentinel (`DOWNGRD` plus one byte) in the last 8 bytes of its random value, which 1.3 clients check.

Deployment showed a different problem: **middleboxes** that inspected TLS broke on anything unfamiliar. TLS 1.3 therefore disguises itself. The legacy version field still says 1.2 (`0x0303`), the real version goes in a `supported_versions` extension, and dummy ChangeCipherSpec messages are sent so the handshake looks like a resumed 1.2 session. QUIC reduces exposed protocol details with packet encryption and partial header protection, while fields such as connection IDs and version remain visible.

## Resumption and 0-RTT

After a handshake, the server can issue a **session ticket**: an opaque identity associated with a resumption PSK. The client derives that PSK from resumption secrets and the ticket nonce; the ticket is not simply the raw key. A resumed handshake skips the certificate.

With a ticket, the client may also send **0-RTT early data** in its very first flight, encrypted with a key derived from the PSK. The catch is serious:

> [!warning] 0-RTT data can be replayed
> An attacker can capture the first flight and send it again. TLS does not inherently guarantee non-replay of early data. Servers can implement anti-replay state, but applications must account for the remaining risk across instances and retries. Early data lacks forward secrecy against later compromise of its PSK. Permit only requests whose actual semantics tolerate replay; an HTTP method label or idempotence alone is not a complete safety argument. A server can answer HTTP `425 Too Early` to make the client retry after the full handshake.

This is lesson 1's replay attack again, accepted deliberately in exchange for speed.

## Certificate chains

A certificate binds a public key to names, and is signed by a **certificate authority** (CA). Clients use configured **trust anchors**, often from a browser, operating system or application root store. Store membership varies. Root private keys can be kept offline while intermediate CAs perform routine issuance; this is an operational design, not a property of every CA.

The following chain-shaped example illustrates a leaf, intermediate and cross-signed root. It is not a live assertion of what `www.rfc-editor.org` currently serves:

```
0 leaf:  CN=rfc-editor.org
         issued by WE1
1 inter: WE1 (Google Trust Services)
         issued by GTS Root R4
2 cross: GTS Root R4
         issued by GlobalSign Root CA
```

The server sends its leaf and needed intermediates. A client must independently trust a suitable anchor. Item 2 illustrates a **cross-signed certificate** for the same subject/key, with a different issuer and potentially different constraints, enabling an alternate path where supported.

Certificate validation includes the following checks (this is not an exhaustive validation algorithm; path-length/name constraints and unsupported critical extensions also matter):

1. Each signature verifies with the issuer's public key, up to a root it trusts.
2. The leaf and intermediate certificates in the validation path are within their validity dates; trust-anchor handling is a separate client-policy input.
3. The leaf's **Subject Alternative Name** matches the hostname. (Browsers ignore the old Common Name field.)
4. Intermediates are marked as CAs (`basicConstraints CA:TRUE`) and allowed to issue.
5. The leaf is allowed for server authentication (extended key usage).
6. Applicable browser policies require **Certificate Transparency** evidence for publicly trusted certificates. A signed certificate timestamp is a log's promise to include the certificate, not itself an inclusion proof; SCTs need not be embedded in the certificate. Monitoring helps detect misissuance.

> [!example] "It works in Chrome but not in curl"
> The server sends only its leaf, not the intermediate. Desktop browsers often cope, because they cache intermediates or fetch them from a URL in the certificate. Other clients may fail with "unable to get local issuer certificate"; fetching and caching depend on the TLS backend, trust store and configuration, not just the application name. The fix is on the server: serve the full chain (leaf plus intermediates).

### Revocation and short lifetimes

If a private key leaks, the certificate must be **revoked**. The two classic mechanisms are **CRLs** (lists of revoked serial numbers) and **OCSP** (ask the CA about one certificate). Direct OCSP requests can reveal certificate lookups to the responder. Some clients **soft-fail** when status cannot be retrieved; others use different revocation mechanisms or policies. Blocking a responder can therefore undermine a soft-fail check. **OCSP stapling** lets the server attach a recent signed OCSP response itself.

The industry's answer has shifted to **short-lived certificates**. Let's Encrypt shut down its OCSP service in 2025 in favour of CRLs. The CA/Browser Forum has cut the maximum lifetime of public certificates from 398 days to 200 days (from March 2026), falling to 100 days in 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Short lifetimes limit the damage of an unrevoked key, and make reliable renewal and monitoring more demanding. **Automated renewal** (for example ACME) is a practical approach, not a mathematical requirement imposed by the lifetime alone.

Checking a server by hand:

```python
import socket, ssl

host = "www.rfc-editor.org"
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()

with socket.create_connection(
        (host, 443), timeout=10) as raw:
    with ctx.wrap_socket(
            raw,
            server_hostname=host) as tls:
        print(tls.version())
        print(tls.cipher()[0])
        cert = tls.getpeercert()
        subject = dict(
            x[0] for x in cert["subject"])
        print(subject)
```

The negotiated version, cipher and certificate subject depend on the live endpoint and local TLS stack; no fixed output is guaranteed. `create_default_context()` turns on chain and hostname verification; passing `server_hostname` sets SNI and the name to check. Code that sets `verify=False` (in `requests`) or `CERT_NONE` throws all of that away and is open to any MITM.

## Encrypted Client Hello

Even with TLS 1.3, the ClientHello is sent in clear, so the SNI reveals the site to anyone on the path, and is widely used for censorship and filtering. **Encrypted Client Hello** (ECH, RFC 9849, 2026) closes that gap:

```
ClientHelloOuter (clear)
  SNI = cloudflare-ech.com  <- public
  ech = HPKE(ClientHelloInner)
ClientHelloInner (encrypted)
  SNI = secret-site.example
```

1. The client looks up the site's DNS **HTTPS record**, which carries an `ECHConfig`: a public key and a **public name** for the provider's client-facing server.
2. It encrypts the real ClientHello with that key and wraps it in an outer ClientHello naming only the public name.
3. The provider decrypts the inner hello and completes the handshake for the real site.

ECH hides the inner ClientHello from passive observers, but the practical anonymity set depends on shared configuration, IP addresses and other metadata; a CDN is not a protocol requirement. Plaintext DNS can independently disclose the requested name. Encrypted DNS protects that hop but does not conceal it from the chosen resolver. For defenders it is a trade-off: firewalls and filters that block by SNI (lesson 6) lose that signal.

## Mutual TLS

In a full server-certificate TLS handshake, the client need not supply a certificate and may authenticate at the application layer later. For certificate-based **mutual TLS (mTLS)**, the server requests a client certificate and the client supplies Certificate and CertificateVerify when authenticating. PSK resumption does not repeat these certificate messages.

```
Server: {CertificateRequest} ...
Client: {Certificate}
        {CertificateVerify}
        {Finished}
```

Where it is used:

- **Service-to-service** traffic in zero trust designs (lesson 2). Configured service meshes can issue workload certificates and apply mTLS. For example, Istio uses SPIFFE-style identities and separate authentication/authorisation policies; permissive modes and unenrolled workloads require attention.
- **APIs** for banks and payment networks, IoT devices and internal admin tools.

Trade-offs and pitfalls:

- You usually run a **private CA**, and must issue, rotate and revoke certificates for every client. Automation is the whole game.
- A certificate proves **who** the caller is, not **what** they may do. You still need authorisation: "service `checkout` may call `POST /charge`".
- TLS terminated at a load balancer ends the mTLS there; the backend must trust the balancer to pass on the verified identity, usually in a header that clients must not be able to set themselves.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> A universal trusted-root count, live endpoint chain/output, certificate-outage frequency and current key-exchange adoption percentages are not asserted: no reproducible dated measurements were available for those claims in this review. The handshake and chain examples are explanatory models.

## Key takeaways
- The illustrated TLS 1.3 certificate handshake provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication in one TLS round trip. Forward secrecy depends on the negotiated mode and secret handling; PSK-only and early data are important exceptions.
- CertificateVerify binds proof of the private key to the transcript. Finished authenticates the negotiated transcript, and downgrade sentinels protect relevant cross-version cases.
- 0-RTT early data is replayable; require application-specific replay-safe semantics and correct intermediary handling.
- Clients validate the chain up to a trusted root, check names and dates, and need the server to send its intermediates; revocation behavior varies, and the public Web PKI lifetime schedule reaches 47 days in 2029.
- ECH encrypts the ClientHello, hiding SNI behind a provider's public name; mTLS authenticates clients with certificates and underpins service-to-service zero trust.
